thread.title: Montana State University releases Zero Waste report highlighting campus recycling progress
thread.title_full: Montana State University releases Zero Waste report highlighting campus recycling progress

author: big sky times
title: Montana State University releases Zero Waste report highlighting campus recycling progress
text:
Montana State University released its first Zero Waste Report on Apr. 22, outlining recent efforts to improve recycling and reduce landfill waste on campus. The report was prepared by Garrett Wright, the university’s first Zero Waste coordinator, who began his role in July.
The initiative is part of MSU’s goal to become a Zero Waste Campus by 2035, meaning at least 90% of campus-generated waste will be diverted from landfills. This effort reflects the university’s commitment to sustainability and environmental responsibility.
Wright said that during Move-In 2025, his team worked with the Residence Hall Association and volunteers to help new students dispose of packing materials properly. “I’m super, super proud to say that we had 0% cardboard contamination for all of the 2025 Move-In, and we also reduced trash campus-wide by 21,000 pounds in the month of August over the year before,” Wright said. He explained that improper disposal can lead to entire dumpsters being sent to landfills if recyclables are contaminated: “If people throw all the Styrofoam and plastic back in the cardboard box, now it’s not recyclable – it’s contaminated. And if there’s too much contamination, an entire 10-yard roll-off (dumpster) could just be tossed in the trash.”
The report details three main strategies: fostering a culture shift through education and outreach events like Move-In recycling campaigns; promoting sustainable product purchases such as compostable materials used by Culinary Services; and increasing infrastructure so everyone can make “a zero-waste decision.” Examples include new compost bins installed in Herrick Hall and Marsh Laboratory.
According to Wright, these measures have already shown results. In the first nine months of this fiscal year starting last July, MSU recycled or composted an additional 124,000 pounds of material compared with fiscal year 2025 while sending about 85,274 fewer pounds to landfill. The average diversion rate through March reached 32.5%. Student interns have supported these efforts—Madeline Ayala helped equip residence hall rooms with personal-size bins labeled for recyclables as part of a pilot project aiming for broader adoption.
MSU tracks its waste diversion rates monthly using data from solid waste vendors and shares this information across various departments so units like housing or sports facilities can monitor their own progress.
“This is a university – it’s about education. That increased enthusiasm about being part of something is awesome to see, and that’s how you create long-lasting change,” Wright said.
MSU leads research funding statewide with annual expenditures exceeding $288 million according to its official website. The university contributes through volunteerism and research aimed at improving lives and protecting environments according to its official website. It ranks among the top five percent globally per Center for World University Rankings according to its official website, enrolling approximately 17,165 students split evenly between residents and nonresidents according to its official website. As Montana’s land-grant institution focused on research, education and outreach according to its official website, MSU extends influence throughout Montana—and beyond according to its official website.
